match.reason: The bank points teach how to structure an essay's paragraphs and conclusion, while the new point is about judging the reasoning in spoken arguments (such as hasty generalisation or attacking the person), so no bank point teaches the same idea.

draft.title: Evaluating arguments
card: Listen or read closely, then ask questions about the argument. Does the evidence really support the claim? Is anything left out?
a claim about a whole group based on one or a few cases. One rude waiter does not show that all waiters are rude.
going after the person instead of the idea. Saying a speaker is silly does not show that their point is wrong.
Spotting a flaw like these shows that an argument is weak. It does not prove the conclusion is false, only that the reasons given do not support it.
draft.remember: Question the evidence and the reasoning, not just the speaker.

a.q: A speaker says her cousin failed after using one app, so the app makes everyone fail. What is the flaw?
opts: A hasty generalisation from one case
A personal attack on the app's maker
A claim with no evidence at all
A reasoned claim backed by many cases
a.why: One cousin's result is used to make a claim about everyone. That is a hasty generalisation. It is not a personal attack, because no person is criticised in place of the idea.
a.clue: How many cases does the speaker use?

b.q: Sam argues for a longer lunch break. Ravi replies, "Sam is always late, so ignore his idea." What is the best evaluation of Ravi's reply?
opts: It attacks Sam, not the idea about lunch
It shows the lunch idea is false
It generalises from many cases of lateness
It answers Sam's reasons with better evidence
b.why: Ravi targets Sam's habits, which have no link to whether a longer lunch is a good idea. That is a personal attack. It does not show the idea is false, because the idea itself is never tested.
b.clue: Does Ravi say anything about lunch breaks?

a.best: A hasty generalisation from one case

b.best: It attacks Sam, not the idea about lunch

problems.detail: 'Not just the speaker' suggests questioning the speaker is also part of evaluating, which muddies the card's point that attacking the person instead of the idea is a flaw. Something like 'Question the evidence and reasoning, not the speaker' would match the card.

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are accurate, with one clear answer each. The remember line's 'not just the speaker' slightly blurs the card's warning against personal attacks.
